content: Albert Calmette, whose full name was Léon Charles Albert Calmette, was a French physician, bacteriologist, and immunologist, born on July 12, 1863, in Nice, France. He played a significant role as an officer of the Pasteur Institute and made groundbreaking contributions to medical science. He is best known for discovering Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG), an attenuated form of Mycobacterium used in the BCG vaccine to prevent tuberculosis. Additionally, he developed the first antivenin for snake venom, known as Calmette's serum. Calmette initially aspired to serve in the Navy as a physician and joined the School of Naval Physicians in Brest in 1881. By 1883, he began his service in the Naval Medical Corps in Hong Kong, where he conducted research on malaria and earned his doctoral degree in 1886. Subsequently, he was stationed in Saint-Pierre and Miquelon in 1887 and later served in West Africa, including Gabon and the French Congo. During this time, he conducted research on malaria, sleeping sickness, and pellagra. Upon returning to France in 1890, Calmette met Louis Pasteur and Émile Roux, the latter becoming his professor in bacteriology. Pasteur entrusted him with the task of founding and directing a branch of the Pasteur Institute in Saigon (French Indochina) in 1891. There, Calmette focused on toxicology, a field closely linked to immunology, and studied snake and bee venom, plant poisons, and curare. He also organized the production of vaccines for smallpox and rabies and conducted research on cholera, as well as the fermentation of opium and rice. In 1894, Calmette returned to France and developed the first antivenoms for snake bites using immune sera derived from vaccinated horses. This work was later expanded by Brazilian physician Vital Brazil at the Instituto Butantan in São Paulo, who developed additional antivenoms for snakes, scorpions, and spiders. Calmette also contributed to the development of the first immune serum against the bubonic plague in collaboration with Alexandre Yersin, who had discovered the plague-causing bacterium Yersinia pestis. Calmette traveled to Portugal to study and assist in combating a plague epidemic in Oporto. In 1895, Émile Roux appointed Calmette as the director of the Pasteur Institute's branch in Lille, where he remained for 25 years. In 1901, he established the first antituberculosis dispensary in Lille, naming it after Émile Roux. He also founded the Ligue du Nord contre la Tuberculose (Northern Antituberculosis League) in 1904, which continues to exist today. In 1909, he helped establish a branch of the Pasteur Institute in Algiers, Algeria. By 1918, he accepted the position of assistant director of the Pasteur Institute in Paris. Calmette's most renowned scientific achievement was his work on developing a vaccine against tuberculosis, a disease that was a leading cause of death at the time. In 1882, German microbiologist Robert Koch had identified Mycobacterium tuberculosis as the causative agent of the disease. Inspired by Koch's discovery and Pasteur's methods, Calmette collaborated with veterinarian and immunologist Camille Guérin. In 1906, Guérin demonstrated that immunity to tuberculosis was associated with the presence of live tubercle bacilli in the blood. Together, Calmette and Guérin worked to develop an attenuated strain of bovine tubercle bacilli that could induce immunity without causing disease. This preparation, named Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG), was achieved by cultivating the bacilli in a bile-containing medium, an idea proposed by Norwegian researcher Kristian Feyer Andvord. From 1908 to 1921, Calmette and Guérin progressively attenuated the virulence of the bacilli through successive cultures. In 1921, they successfully used BCG to vaccinate newborn infants at the Charité hospital in Paris. However, the vaccination program faced a major setback in 1930 when 72 vaccinated children in Lübeck, Germany, developed tuberculosis due to contamination of vaccine batches. This incident temporarily halted mass vaccination programs. By 1932, safer production techniques were implemented, and mass vaccination resumed in many countries. Despite this success, the Lübeck tragedy deeply affected Calmette, and he passed away in Paris in 1933, one year after the incident. Albert Calmette was also the brother of Gaston Calmette, the editor of Le Figaro, who was tragically murdered in 1914 by Henriette Caillaux, the wife of Finance Minister Joseph Caillaux.
